# The Unmatched Pool

**Industry:** [[music-distribution-platforms|Music Distribution Platforms]]
**Type:** High Impact
**One-liner:** Money is generated by streams whose underlying compositions cannot be matched to their writers, accumulates in pools, and is eventually distributed by market share to people who did not write the songs.
**Tags:** #graph-neural-networks #bert #word-embeddings #k-nearest-neighbors #gradient-boosting #evaluation-metrics #feature-engineering #compliance

## The Problem
A stream generates two royalties. One belongs to the owner of the sound recording, identified by an ISRC, which the distributor supplies and which is generally reliable. The other belongs to the writers and publishers of the musical composition, identified by an ISWC, which is administered by an entirely different set of organisations.

Nothing authoritative links the two. A recording's ISRC does not carry the composition's identity. The link exists only where someone registered it, and registration depends on writers, publishers and administrators filing accurate claims — across societies, territories and collecting bodies, in formats with inconsistent name handling, alternate spellings, pseudonyms and varying split conventions.

When the link is missing or contested, the mechanical royalty cannot be paid. It accumulates. The Mechanical Licensing Collective was established in part to administer exactly this and inherited a historical unmatched pool measured in hundreds of millions of dollars.

The eventual treatment of unmatched money is where the industry's dispute lives. Where it cannot be matched after a defined period, it is distributed by market share, which routes it to the largest rights holders rather than to the people who wrote the unmatched songs. Those two populations are not the same, and the people most likely to be unmatched — independent writers, small catalogues, international repertoire, older recordings — are systematically the people with least capacity to file a claim.

Matching failures are ordinary. A writer credited as "Rob" on one filing and "Robert" on another. A title with a parenthetical remix suffix. A featured artist recorded as a writer. Splits that do not total one hundred percent. A cover version registered without reference to the original composition. A sample cleared verbally and never registered.

The distributor is where much of this originates, because it is where the metadata is first captured — from an artist filling in a web form, often with no understanding of the difference between a recording and a composition.

## Why It's Unsolved
The two rights were administered separately for a century and the systems reflect that. Recording data lives with labels and distributors; composition data lives with publishers and collecting societies; the standards, identifiers and organisations differ and there is no authoritative crosswalk.

Nobody is paid to fix it. A distributor is compensated for delivering recordings, not for ensuring the composition's writers are identified. A collecting society is funded by what it distributes. The unmatched pool's eventual market-share distribution means the largest participants are not harmed by the failure, and are in fact its beneficiaries. There is no party whose revenue depends on matching improving, which is the entire explanation for why it has not.

Matching is a genuinely hard entity resolution problem at enormous scale. Tens of millions of recordings against tens of millions of compositions, with noisy names, inconsistent titles, multiple languages and transliterations, and legitimate ambiguity where different songs share a title.

And the incentive to claim aggressively is real. A system that resolves ambiguity generously invites claims on works the claimant did not write, which has happened and is a serious problem in its own right, so conservatism in matching is partly a fraud control.

## What a Solution Looks Like
Capture the link at the point of origin. A distributor uploading a recording is the one moment where the recording and its composition are both known to someone. Asking better questions at upload, validating against known compositions, and resolving the writer identities then rather than later is by far the cheapest available intervention and is nobody's product requirement.

Entity resolution as a graph, not a string comparison. Writers, works, recordings, publishers and societies form a graph with many corroborating edges — co-writing relationships, publisher affiliations, catalogue co-occurrence, recording metadata — and resolution on that structure is far stronger than name matching, which is what most current processes do.

Audio-based composition identification for the cases metadata cannot solve. A cover, a live version or a re-recording is identifiable as the same composition from the audio itself, and melodic similarity matching is mature enough to propose candidate links for human confirmation.

Confidence-tiered matching with a review path. High-confidence matches paid automatically, ambiguous ones surfaced to the claimants involved for resolution, rather than a binary matched-or-pooled outcome that sends ambiguity straight to the pool.

Transparency on the unmatched. A searchable public view of what is unmatched and why lets writers find their own money, which is the simplest remedy available and would be uncomfortable for exactly the reason it would work.

## Impact If Solved
Hundreds of millions of dollars are misdirected by a matching failure that no participant is paid to fix, and the cost falls on the writers least able to pursue it. The data required to fix it sits with distributors and collecting societies in quantities that make the entity resolution tractable, and the highest-leverage intervention — resolving the link at upload — costs a better form and a validation step.
